entry.title: Killam v. MaineHealth
entry.content:
STATE OF MAINE APPELLATE DIVISON WORKERS’ COMPENSATION BOARD Case No. App. Div. 25-0013 Decision No. 26-08
TAMMIE L. (COOMBS) KILLAM (Appellee)
v.
MAINEHEALTH (Appellant)
and
SYNERNET (Insurer)
Conference held: April 8, 2026 Decided: August 27, 2026
PANEL MEMBERS: Administrative Law Judges Stovall, Rooks, and Smith By: Administrative Law Judge Smith
[¶1] MaineHealth/Maine Coast Memorial Hospital (the Hospital) appeals from a decision of a Workers’ Compensation Board administrative law judge (Hirtle, ALJ) denying the Hospital’s Petition for Review pertaining to Tammie Killam’s July 2, 2014 , work injury. The Hospital co ntends the ALJ erred by interpreting the independent medical examiner’s (IME’S) opinion to contain an “unambiguous” assessment of no work capacity , and by adopting that interpretation . We disagree and affirm the decision. I. BACKGROUND [¶2] Tammie Killam was hired by the Hospital as a full -time orderly on October 21, 2013. On July 2, 2014, while moving a table in the operating room, she 2
felt and heard a pop on the ulnar side of her let wrist. As established in a consent decree dated March 7, 2018 , Ms. Killam sustained a work-related left wrist injury on July 2, 2014, and resulting “psychological overlay consistent with an adjustment disorder with depression and anxiety.” The parties agreed she was entitled to receive total incapacity benefits without prejudice, pursuant to 39-A M.R.S.A. § 212. [¶3] In 2020, the Hospital filed a Petition for Review and sought to reduce Ms. Killam’s level of benefits to reflect a full-time, minimum wage -earning capacity. Ms. Killam then filed a Petition for Payment of Medical and Related Services. The ALJ found in a decree dated August 11, 2022, that Ms. Killam had developed causally related symptoms and limitations in her right wrist and remained totally incapacitated to earn because of her work-related injury and its psychological sequela

entry.content:

  • Online Services |
  • Help |

DHHS → Office of MaineCare Services (OMS) → Provider Resources → MaineCare Comprehensive Benchmarking Report Initiation Notice

MaineCare Comprehensive Benchmarking Report Initiation Notice

Aug 31, 2026

The Department initiated a comprehensive rate benchmarking report, as required by MRS Title 22 §3173-J. Rate reform law requires that, every four years, the Department compare MaineCare rates to the rates paid by the following:

  • Medicare
  • At least five comparison Medicaid states
  • Any appropriate Maine commercial payers

Interested parties will have the opportunity for public review and comment. The final report will be available on the MaineCare Rate System Reform webpage.

For questions please contact Megan Scott, MaineCare’s Legislative and Reform Coordinator.

*This notice is provided pursuant to Public Law 2022, Chapter 639.

entry.title: Looking Ahead: Eligibility-Dedicated Data Feed to Support MaineCare Renewals and Enrollment
entry.content:
Maine.gov

  • Agencies |
  • Online Services |
  • Help |
  • Search Maine.gov

DHHS → Office of MaineCare Services (OMS) → Provider Resources → Looking Ahead: Eligibility-Dedicated Data Feed to Support MaineCare Renewals and Enrollment

Looking Ahead: Eligibility-Dedicated Data Feed to Support MaineCare Renewals and Enrollment

Sep 04, 2026

Two weeks ago, we announced communications support for MaineCare partners and providers regarding changes the federal government is making to MaineCare (Maine’s Medicaid program) eligibility. This message provides an early look at planned data-sharing that will help the Maine Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) verify information needed for MaineCare eligibility. Our goal is to help eligible Mainers keep their coverage and access to services with as little disruption as possible.

No action is needed now. We are sharing this information early to make providers aware of what is being planned. We will share more information as plans and timelines are finalized.

DHHS will continue to use administrative data sources it has access to as much as possible to support automatic (“passive”) renewals for MaineCare members. Federal changes to eligibility mean we need additional information to help more eligible members maintain their MaineCare coverage. This data will help Mainers continue to benefit from MaineCare, which in turn will help providers minimize the impact of these federal Medicaid cuts on their revenue and on their charity and uncompensated care.

Clinical Data Will Help People Stay Enrolled in MaineCare

Electronic health record (EHR) systems contain clinical data that Maine and numerous other states are planning to use to help exempt Medicaid applicants and members with work-limiting health conditions from Work Requirements. In Maine, this data will support MaineCare eligibility determination activities administered by the Office for Family Independence (OFI). DHHS intends to partner with providers to collect this information through HealthInfoNet, the State’s contractor for this work. HealthInfoNet will identify indicators of exemptions from work requirements by collecting and processing this clinical data from providers. Using clinical data alongside claims and other administrative data to generate more timely and comprehensive information will help keep Mainers enrolled in MaineCare. We will refer to the data sent to HealthInfoNet for this purpose as the eligibility-dedicated clinical data feed.

Until the eligibility-dedicated clinical data feed is established we will be basing automatic exceptions for work-limiting health conditions on claims data alone in order to meet implementation deadlines.

This Data Sharing Will Be Separate from the Health Information Exchange

The eligibility-dedicated clinical data feed will be separate from the health information exchange (HIE) data that many providers already share with HealthInfoNet.

The eligibility-dedicated data feed will include only the information needed to support MaineCare eligibility activities. This information will be stored separately from HIE data. It will not be available through HealthInfoNet’s clinical portal or through analytics tools used by some provider organizations. The eligibility-dedicated clinical data feed will be used only in support of OMS and OFI activities associated with eligibility.

Key details to note:

  • The steps needed for a provider to establish this new data feed will vary by provider organization. For example, some provider organizations already have a data feed with HealthInfoNet that can be used as a starting point. Capabilities of the organization’s EHR vendor or technology support may also affect the work needed to establish the data feed. Providers eligible for relevant Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP) funding may consider using this funding for these costs, as determined by the allowable uses of specific RHTP opportunities.
  • We expect it will take the majority of provider organizations two to four months to build their eligibility-dedicated clinical data feed with HealthInfoNet. This time range will be dependent on provider organization’s or vendor’s availability to engage with HealthInfoNet. We expect it will take less time than building a typical HIE data sharing connection with HealthInfoNet.
  • Clinical care teams are not expected to need to take additional steps to send this information as part of their day-to-day work. Once the data feed is established, the identified data categories will be shared automatically with HealthInfoNet.
  • Broad categories of exemptions in statute for work-limiting health conditions include those who are blind or disabled, have a substance use disorder, disabling mental disorder, or complex medical condition. DHHS continues to work with the federal government to clarify data related to these categories that may assist states to automatically exempt individuals, including information related to a person’s ability to work. Kinds of data may include demographic information, diagnosis indicators, encounter or event indicators, and billing codes, among others.

More Information Will Be Coming – No Action Needed Now The Department and HealthInfoNet will distribute instructions for provider organizations to opt into this initiative and implement the eligibility-dedicated data feed. Future communications will include information such as:

  • Which provider types will be prioritized for establishing these connections
  • How providers can participate
  • The types of information that will be needed
  • Technical requirements and specifications
  • Onboarding and implementation steps
  • Timelines
  • Testing procedures
  • Contacts for technical and operational qu

entry.title: Management Track Assessment for American Plaice and Gulf of Maine Haddock; Public Meeting
entry.content: NMFS will convene the Management Track Assessment Peer Review Meeting for the purpose of reviewing American plaice and Gulf of Maine haddock stocks. The Management Track Assessment Peer Review is a formal scientific peer-review process for evaluating and presenting stock assessment results to managers for fish stocks in the offshore U.S. waters of the northwest Atlantic. Assessments are prepared by the lead stock assessment scientist and reviewed by an independent panel of stock assessment experts. The public is invited to attend the presentations and discussions between the review panel and the scientists who have participated in the stock assessment process.

entry.title: Temporary Changes to Referral and Authorization Processes Ending November 30, 2026
entry.content:
Maine.gov

  • Agencies |
  • Online Services |
  • Help |
  • Search Maine.gov

DHHS → Office of MaineCare Services (OMS) → Provider Resources → Temporary Changes to Referral and Authorization Processes Ending November 30, 2026

Temporary Changes to Referral and Authorization Processes Ending November 30, 2026

Sep 08, 2026

Beginning December 1, 2026, the Department will require members to complete a Single Assessment within the past 12 months before processing referrals, prior authorization requests, and continued stay reviews for children’s medium- and high-intensity services. 

As previously communicated, the Department temporarily reinstated direct-to-provider referral and prior authorization processes while operational challenges with the Single Assessment process were being addressed. That temporary process will end November 30, 2026. 

The Single Assessment process has stabilized significantly, with assessments now completed in an average of 7.5 business days after a request is submitted. 

Thank you for your continued partnership with the Single Assessment process.

entry.title: Maine Logger’s Day - October 12
entry.content:
WHEREAS, the logging industry has served as an economic driver and cultural tradition in Maine for centuries; and

WHEREAS, the logging industry creates rural jobs and provides revenue for local communities, contributing $534 million to the state’s economy annually; and

WHEREAS, loggers provide renewable material for products used by people in Maine every day; and

WHEREAS, loggers are the root of Maine’s $8.3 billion forest economy; and

WHEREAS, loggers are the means by which healthy and responsible forest management plans are accomplished; and

WHEREAS, logging helps keep Maine’s forests healthy, which support vital animal habitats, protect watersheds, sequester carbon, provide recreational opportunities, and limit wildfires; and

WHEREAS, logging provides for healthy forests through regeneration to ensure the sustainability of the industry for future generations of Maine people;

NOW THEREFORE, be it resolved that I, Janet T. Mills, Governor of the State of Maine, do hereby proclaim October 12, 2026 as 

Maine Logger’s Day

throughout the State of Maine, and I urge all citizens to recognize this observance. 

In testimony whereof, I have caused

the Great Seal of the State to be

hereunto affixed GIVEN under my

hand at Augusta this tenth day 
of September Two Thousand Twenty-Six

entry.title: Pung v. Isabella County
entry.content: PRELIMINARY PRINT Volume 609 U. S. Part 1 Pages 30–58 OFFICIAL REPORTS OF THE SUPREME COURT June 23, 2026 REBECCA A. WOMELDORF reporter of decisions Page Proof Pending Publication NOTICE: This preliminary print is subject to formal revision before the bound volume is published. Users are requested to notify the Reporter of Decisions, Supreme Court of the United States, Washington, D. C. 20543, pio@supremecourt.gov, of any typographical or other formal errors. 30 OCTOBER TERM, 2025 Syllabus PUNG, PERSONAL REPRESENTATIVE OF THE ESTATE OF PUNG v. ISABELLA COUNTY, MICHIGAN certiorari to the united states court of appeals for the sixth circuit No. 25–95. Argued February 25, 2026—Decided June 23, 2026 The Pung family owed $2,241.93 in real-property taxes, so local tax author- ities in Isabella County, Michigan, initiated foreclosure proceedings and sold the Pung home—which was assessed at $194,400 for tax purposes— for $76,008 at public auction. Michael Pung sued in Federal court, and the District Court granted Pung partial summary judgment on his Fifth Amendment claim. The court held that Pung should receive only the surplus proceeds from the tax sale—i. e., the difference between the sale price and the tax debt—not the property's fair market value. The District Court also rejected Pung's claim under the Eighth Amendment Excessive Fines Clause. The Sixth Circuit affrmed. Held: 1. The proper baseline for measuring “just compensation” following a tax sale is the auction sale price, not the property's hypothetical fair market value, at least when the sale is fairly conducted in light of the country's history of tax sales. Pp. 35–43. (a) For hundreds of years, English and American law have allowed the seizure and sale of property as a tax-collection method, provided that the government return any surplus proceeds to the debtor. Argued April 27, 2026—Decided June 25, 2026 Monsanto Company manufactures and distributes Roundup, a glyphosate- based herbicide designed to control weeds. The EPA has repeatedly evaluated glyphosate and repeatedly concluded that glyphosate is not likely to cause cancer. EPA's assessment is shared by many other regu- latory bodies around the world. In accordance with EPA's view that glyphosate is not likely to cause cancer in humans, EPA has not required labels on glyphosate-based pesticides like Roundup to include a cancer warning. In 2019, John Durnell sued Monsanto in Missouri state court, alleging that he had used Monsanto's Roundup products for about 20 years and that they had caused his non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. As relevant here, Durnell brought a failure-to-warn tort claim, asserting that Monsanto should have included a cancer warning on Roundup's label. A jury agreed and awarded Durnell more than $1 million on the failure-to-warn theory. On appeal, the Missouri Court of Appeals affrmed, 707 S. W. 3d 828. The Court of Appeals rejected Monsanto's argument that the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act expressly pre- empted Durnell's failure-to-warn claim, see 7 U. S. C. § 136v(b). Maine Paid Family and Medical Leave Program Publishes Actuarial Report, First Claims Report

October 1, 2026

For Immediate Release: Oct. 1, 2026

Media Contact: Autumn Mahoney, Communications Specialist media.dol@maine.gov

Actuarial report projects PFML Trust Fund will remain stable for the next 10 years

AUGUSTA - The Maine Paid Family and Medical Leave (PFML) program has published its second annual actuarial report, as well as its first claims report on Oct. 1, 2026.

PFML became law in 2023 and is a statewide program that provides eligible workers with up to 12 weeks of paid leave for medical, parental, family care, military family or safe leave.

The PFML program began accepting claims on March 30, 2026, and began paying benefits on May 1, 2026. This initial claims report covers the program's first three months of claims activity, from March 30 through June 30, 2026. Future claims reports will be published annually and will cover a full year of claims activity.

Highlights of the reports include:

  • The PFML Trust Fund remains solvent and based on updated revenue and claim expenditure, is projected to remain stable for the next 10 years.
  • The program received 8,376 applications between March 30 and June 30, 2026.
  • Among the claims approved, medical leave was the most common reason, followed by welcoming a new child and caring for a family member. Other leave reasons represented a very small portion of the overall claim volume.

"We are excited to see the PFML Program effectively off the ground and helping Maine workers and businesses through life's big moments, both now and for years to come," said PFML Director Luke Monahan.

More information on the PFML program, including how to apply, can be found on the program's website: https://www.maine.gov/paidleave/

Employees, employers and self-employed individuals with questions can call 207-621-5024 between8 a.m. and 5 p.m. Monday through Friday. Employees can send a message through the Benefits Application Portal, while employers and self-employed individuals can send a message through the Maine Paid Leave Contributions Portal.

entry.title: US Labor Department finds railroad illegally terminated employee who refused to work during severe weather
entry.content: LITTLE ROCK, AR – A U.S. Department of Labor Occupational Safety and Health Administration whistleblower investigation has concluded that Union Pacific Railroad Co. violated the Federal Railroad Safety Act when it removed from service and later terminated a North Little Rock yardman who notified management of nearby lightning and federal safety standards. OSHA determined that the employee voiced concerns about nearby lightning, cited OSHA and NOAA lightening safety guidelines, initiated a safety stand-down, and refused to work until the storm passed. Within minutes of the stand-down, Union Pacific removed the employee from service and was later charged with insubordination. Union Pacific terminated his employment on May 30, 2024.On June 10, 2026, OSHA ordered Union Pacific to remove from the employee’s employment records any reference of the incident, and pay back wages, lost benefits, compensatory and punitive damages totaling at least $304,869, and attorney’s fees. Union Pacific filed objections to OSHA’s order and has requested a hearing before a U.S. Department of Labor Administrative Law Judge.OSHA’s Whistleblower Protection Program enforces 25 whistleblower statutes that protect employees from retaliation for reporting violations of workplace airline, anti-money laundering, commercial motor carrier, consumer product, criminal antitrust, environmental, financial reform, food safety, health insurance reform, maritime, motor vehicle safety, nuclear, pipeline, public transportation agency, railroad, safety and health, securities, and tax laws.Editor’s note: The U.S. Department of Labor does not release the names of employees involved in whistleblower complaints.

Temporary Changes to Referral and Authorization Processes Ending November 30, 2026

Oct 06, 2026

Beginning December 1, 2026, the Department will require members to complete a Single Assessment within the past 12 months before processing referrals, prior authorization requests, and continued stay reviews for children’s medium- and high-intensity services. 

As previously communicated, the Department temporarily reinstated direct-to-provider referral and prior authorization processes while operational challenges with the Single Assessment process were being addressed. That temporary process will end November 30, 2026. 

The Single Assessment process has stabilized significantly, with assessments now completed in an average of 7.5 business days after a request is submitted. 

Thank you for your continued partnership with the Single Assessment process.
